catalog_quote: Katuic languages are phonologically typical Austroasiatic languages of the lower Mekong region with prosodic words of a maximally disyllabic, iambic template and vowel inventories with nine to eleven vowel qualities (Gehrmann and Conver 2015, Jenny et al. 2015). ... PK words may be monosyllables or disyllables. The final syllable or main syllable of a disyllabic word is always prosodically prominent and phonotactically unrestricted while the penultimate syllable or presyllable is always unstressed and phonotactically restricted with respect to the main syllable. A monosyllable is by definition a main syllable without a presyllable and, therefore, phonotactically equivalent to the main syllable of a disyllabic word. ... The PK phonological word is a maximally disyllabic iamb (cf. Butler 2015a) but not a sesquisyllable in the original sense of the word as coined by Matisoff (1973).
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are at most disyllabic; the final (main) syllable carries the stress and the presyllable is unstressed. This is a family-wide (Katuic) and Proto-Katuic statement, not a description of Lower Ta'oih itself; the only first-hand tto data in print (L-Thongkum 2002, pp. 98-101, broad phonetic transcription) mark primary stress on the final syllable of every disyllable (taˈpat 'six', kaˈcaŋ 'to smile', ŋˈhaaŋ 'bone', parˈʔaw 'thigh'), consistent with the family pattern, but give no rule in prose.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (Gehrmann 2018); no marks in L-Thongkum 2002.
new_statements.exceptions: Gehrmann 2018 p. 138: 'The description of the PK word above does not accurately describe the prosodic word of any one modern Katuic language' -- said of presyllable structure (reduction, sesquisyllabification), not of stress placement. Ta'oiq is listed among languages whose presyllable coda nasals have been reanalysed as prenasalised onsets (Table 8, p. 138).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (maximally disyllabic iamb); citation-form wordlist items in L-Thongkum 2002. Gehrmann's Ta'oiq data (Conver, Conver & Schmutz ms.) is labelled [tth] although Gehrmann & Conver 2015 equate Ta'oiq with the Ong/Ir/Katang type that Glottolog files with tto; the tto-specific evidence is therefore only L-Thongkum's Tha Taeng transcriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Lower Ta'oih [tto] = lowe1395, filed by Glottolog 5.1 under Katuic > Ta'oi > Ong beside Ong-Ir [oog] (ongg1239); Ethnologue alternate name Tong, dialects Tong and Hantong' (quoted in Schmutz 2013: viii). Glottolog's bibliography equates L-Thongkum's 'Ta Oi' of Tha Taeng' (Sekong) with tto, and Gehrmann & Conver 2015 (p. lvi) describe the Ong/Ir/Katang-type Ta'oi ('Ta'oiq', a register language restructuring final stops) as one of the two main Ta'oi languages, which fits L-Thongkum's post-glottalised Ta Oi'. Gehrmann 2018 nevertheless codes his Ta'oiq data (Conver, Conver & Schmutz ms., Champasak) as [tth]. Upper Ta'oih [tth] = uppe1406 (van der Haak 1993 Ta'uaih; Vietnamese Ta-oih of Solntseva 1996 and Nguyen Van Loi 1986, which Gehrmann & Conver place with Pacoh) is a different entity; nothing quoted here comes from those tth sources. Huffman's 1971 Ta-Oi notebook informant (Tasseng Huay Hee, Salavan) is of undetermined variety.
